extracted.intended_audience: literary scholars, translators, editors, and informed readers of Rabelais
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and commentary for judging Rabelais’s works, style, translations, and textual editions — covering moral reception, language and vocabulary, sources, authorship questions, revision methods, and standards for good translation and editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Studied coarseness / occasional grossness
rubrics_metrics.description: The great reproach always brought against Rabelais is not the want of reserve of his language merely, but his occasional studied coarseness, which is enough to spoil his whole work, and which lowers its value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: La Bruyere’s contemporary judgment: where Rabelais is bad 'it goes beyond the worst' yet where it is good 'it reaches the exquisite.' Use this criterion to weigh coarse passages: they may detract from value for some readers. Consider examples and frequency before condemning the whole work; compare with ancients and contemporaries who used frank language. Anti-pattern: dismissing the entire work solely for isolated coarse expressions without historic/contextual consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/contextual appropriateness of language and jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: One must understand the atmosphere in which the book was created and the examples of similar tendencies in literature and popular taste of the time before condemning Rabelais.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare Rabelais to Aristophanes, Catullus, Petronius, Italian comic theatre, Fabliaux, church carvings, and contemporary songs and tales. If coarseness was a common cultural expression, judging by modern standards is misleading. Anti-pattern: treating Rabelais as a unique scapegoat while ignoring common practices of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral effect / absence of pernicious instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Where does he tempt one to stray from duty? Where, even indirectly, does he give pernicious advice? Whom has he led to evil ways? Does he ever inspire feelings that breed misconduct and vice, or is he ever the apologist of these?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether gaiety or frankness produces actual moral harm; author argues Rabelais cannot be accused of actively hurting readers despite coarse language. Use this as a higher-order ethical criterion rather than surface vocabulary counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for different audiences and expurgation
rubrics_metrics.description: Women in particular quickly revolt from him ... if he be read aloud to them, omitting the rougher parts and modernizing the pronunciation, it will be seen that they too are impressed by his lively wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For presenting Rabelais to sensitive audiences or young persons, selective omission of rougher parts and modernization of pronunciation may make admirable passages usable. Anti-pattern: producing modernized rewrites or attempting to 'improve' the original text—expurgated editions that rewrite in modern French are 'fools' for their pains' and insulting to the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporary acceptance and patronage as evidence of value
rubrics_metrics.description: His dedications prove to what extent his whole work was accepted ... privileges from Francis I. and Henry II. and dedications to great lords and princes of the Church show high contemporary appreciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dedications, privileges, papal favor, and patronage as evidence for the work's contemporary reception and legitimacy. Weigh official honors and prominent patrons when assessing historical standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation difficulty — not merely familiarity with French
rubrics_metrics.description: There are few translations of Rabelais in foreign tongues; certainly the task is no light one, and demands more than a familiarity with ordinary French.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that translators need deep linguistic, cultural, and historical knowledge. Consider national obstacles (e.g., Spanish Inquisition) and linguistic affinity (Italian easier than Spanish in principle). Anti-pattern: assuming any competent bilingual can produce an adequate translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation fidelity vs. recasting: fidelity, spirit, and anglicization
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative evaluation of translators: Fischart's work is a recast full of alterations and exaggerations; Urquhart 'feels' the original and renders the sense with force and vivacity; Motteux is precise, elegant, and very faithful but different in character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge translations on (a) fidelity to sense, (b) capture of tone and vivacity, (c) success in naturalizing coinages (anglicization), and (d) whether the translator takes liberties (recasting) or preserves form. Use concrete comparisons: Fischart enlarged coarseness and attacks on Church; Urquhart anglicizes invented words successfully; Motteux is elegant but less spirited. Anti-pattern: valuing literalness alone over liveliness and comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial principle: do not amalgamate variant readings into a fabricated text
rubrics_metrics.description: After Le Duchat, all the editions ... made the mistake of collecting and placing side by side things which had no connection with each other, which had even been substituted for each other. The result was a fabricated text, full of contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good editions should avoid patchwork amalgamations; instead give the latest text accompanied by earlier variations, or alternatively take the first text as basis and note later modifications. Show variations, suppress amalgamation that fabricates a false unified text. Practical guidance: annotate changes, present variants, and resist merging contradictory readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of Rabelais’ multilingual and dialectal vocabulary sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Rabelais had at his command something like three languages ... he took advantage of the happy chances and the richness of the popular speech, but he wrote in French, and nothing but French.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating style, account for mixture of French of the time, provincial dialects, Latin/Greek coinages, and invented words. Avoid provincial claims that attribute his genius solely to local dialect; instead note the composite sources (classical, provincial, popular).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invented words and neologisms as stylistic resource
rubrics_metrics.description: He fabricated words, too, on Greek and Latin models, with great ease, sometimes audaciously and with needless frequency... he coined an enormous number of interminable words, droll expressions, sudden and surprising constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess neologisms by whether they serve humorous or rhetorical effect (mockery, variety, gloss of antique novelty) rather than as gratuitous obscurity. Consider parallels with Aristophanes. Anti-pattern: treating coinage as mere obscurantism without analyzing function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety, lack of unity, and deliberate elaboration of style
rubrics_metrics.description: His romance ... changes the style completely every other moment: it has no constant character or uniform manner, and therefore unity is almost entirely wanting in his work, while his endeavours after contrast are unceasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the work for deliberate contrasts and conscious craft rather than expecting uniformity. Recognize that apparent spontaneity disguises extensive revision and careful insertion. Anti-pattern: criticising the text solely for lack of uniform style without acknowledging deliberate artistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial revision method: small insertions rather than wholesale rewrites
rubrics_metrics.description: When an author recasts some passage ... Rabelais suppressed nothing, modified nothing; he did not change his plan at all. What he did was to make insertions, to slip in between two clauses a new one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For textual scholars: trace insertions to understand how effect was heightened; do not assume major rewrites — look for incremental additions. Use examples like the shipwreck chapter to study craft. Editions should preserve and display these insertions and their stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining authorship by stylistic discrepancy (Chronique question)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chronique Gargantuaine is uniform in style and quite simple, but cannot with certainty be attributed to him ... in the Chronique everything is heavy, occasionally meaningless, and nearly always insipid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stylistic analysis (tone, lucidity, vivacity) to weigh authorship claims but remain cautious: both theories (authorship vs. other author) are defensible. Avoid decisive attribution when evidence is mixed; consider that early drafts or first attempts can differ markedly from mature works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources vs. originality: traceable borrowings do not preclude originality
rubrics_metrics.description: He was familiar with ... the Facetiae of Poggio, and the last sermonnaires ... while gathering his materials wherever he could find them, he was nevertheless profoundly original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating originality, document known sources (Poggio, Pliny, Aristophanes, etc.) but judge the degree of transformation and creative synthesis. Anti-pattern: declaring a work derivative simply because sources can be found; instead show how materials were reworked into something original.

rubrics_metrics.name: National taste and translator’s national treatment affect reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Fischart is much superior to Rabelais in style ... his equal in erudition and in the invention of new expressions ... but he is an imitator rather than a creator. England has been less daring, and her modesty and discretion have brought her success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess translations and adaptations in light of national literary tastes: German recasting/exaggeration (Fischart) vs English naturalizing (Urquhart) vs Motteux’s continuation. Consider how national sensibilities shape both liberties taken and success among readers.
